turns.en: We used to fold a piece of paper and do quick Crazy Eights—8 minutes, 1 minute per idea—to solve some interface problem. What’s the version of that with today’s tooling? You just go explore a couple of tools to figure out the blank-canvas problem. Maybe you open up Paper and use a new tool to do something you’re already familiar with. Maybe you open up Claude Code and vibe code eight quick variations. Or you go even deeper: 'How do I connect Claude Code to Paper’s MCP? How do I actually create a plan in Claude Code and have it executed in Paper’s MCP?' So that when you open Paper, you have eight rough versions of that concept, and you can decide what’s trash and what’s interesting. Just do that, and do it in a way that’s interesting to you. Don’t look for Tommy’s newsletter. Don’t look for the Dive Club newsletter to tell you what to do. Tune it all out, pick up a few things you find curious, practice thinking, and just try it. Start building your own little database of insight around what you’re learning and what you like about your workflow.
turns.zh: 我们会折一张纸，做快速 Crazy Eights，8 分钟、每个想法 1 分钟，来解决某个界面问题。换成今天的工具，这个该怎么玩？你就去试几个工具，弄清楚那张空白画布的问题。也许你打开 Paper，用新工具做你本来就熟悉的事。也许你打开 Claude Code，跟着感觉写八个快速变体。或者你再进一步：'怎么把 Claude Code 接到 Paper 的 MCP 上？怎么在 Claude Code 里做计划，再让它在 Paper 的 MCP 里执行？' 这样一来，等你打开 Paper 的时候，里面已经有八个这个概念的粗糙版本，你可以直接挑哪些是垃圾、哪些有意思。就这么做，并且用你觉得好玩的方式去做。别去看 Tommy 的 newsletter，也别去看 Dive Club 的 newsletter 来琢磨你该干嘛。把那些噪音关掉，挑几件你觉得好奇的东西，练习思考，直接开干。然后开始建立你自己的小洞察库，记录你在学什么、你喜欢工作流里的哪些部分。

turns.en: Because everybody’s workflow—and this is the one thing I’ve seen a lot—is different. If we were to put screenshots of everybody’s workflows up on screen,
turns.zh: 因为每个人的工作流——这是我看过很多次的一点——都不一样。如果我们把所有人的工作流截图放上屏幕，

turns.en: the ones that are emerging, they come in all shapes and sizes—oblong, weird—and they’re just very custom right now.
turns.zh: 那些正在涌现的工作流，形状各异、千奇百怪，而且目前都非常定制化。

turns.en: Yeah, even within an org. The delta between workflows inside an org—I’ve been doing a lot of customer calls, and it’s shocking. Obviously everyone has their own process and ways to tap into creativity, but people are using fundamentally different tools, ways of working, and ways of thinking. The creative design process has spread apart so much that it’s chaotic. And I think there’s a lot of value in the people, teams, and individuals who are just sharing their workflows. And it’s important to remember that this is a good activity right now. You don’t have to frame it as, 'Here’s my workflow, you should do this.' I like to strike 'should' from the vocabulary right now and just compare workflows, compare shapes. Because eventually we will converge around better practices, but we don’t know what those are yet. So right now, the best thing you can do—if you want to get involved in this kind of work—is to find workflows that work for you. Spend maybe 80% of your time on the familiar things that get the work done, and the rest of the time make room for exploration. And for the people I said can wait: we are going to converge around stuff. If you have the luxury of not having to get involved yet, you can wait, and there will probably be a concentration of 'these are the better workflows.'
turns.zh: 对，即使在同一个组织内。组织内部工作流之间的差异——我做了很多客户访谈，真的很震惊。显然每个人都有自己的流程和挖掘创造力的方法，但大家用的工具、工作方式和思维方式根本不同。创意设计流程已经被发散得如此极端，甚至有些混乱。而我认为，那些分享自己工作流的人、团队和个人，价值非常大。而且要记住，现在做这件事是件好事。你不需要把它说成：'这是我的工作流，你应该这么做。' 我现在喜欢把'应该'从词汇表里划掉，只是去比较工作流、比较形状。因为最终我们会围绕更好的实践收敛，但现在还不知道那是什么。所以现在你最好的做法——如果你想参与这类工作——是找到适合自己的工作流。把大概 80% 的时间花在熟悉的事情上，把活干完；剩下的一些时间留给你去探索。而对那些我说可以再等等的人：我们终会收敛。如果你足够幸运，现在还不必参与，你可以等，到时候大概会有一批被公认的'更好的工作流'。

turns.en: I think something that makes our journeys similar—but also unique to the average designer listening—is that we both invested in distribution, putting ideas out there and seeing where it took us. For me, I rode this wave of Figma adding a bunch more technical features. There was this new type of design that honestly felt a bit more like engineering. It was really easy for me to just tinker. I was curious—I just went for it. I tried every little tactic and kept putting ideas out there. And it wasn't 'do this'; it was more like, 'Hey, I tried this, it was cool, I'm going to try it again tomorrow.' I think we're in a moment where that opportunity is wide open again for people who want to grow within the design community. There’s so much hunger for people to see workflows, the 100% different experiments people are running, and the lessons others have learned. If you just show up, try things, be curious, and treat Twitter like a little journal of what you're learning and the experiments you're running—this is the time to reap the rewards of being publicly curious.
turns.zh: 我觉得让我们的旅程相似的，是我们在分发上都做了投资，把想法发出去，看它会带我们去哪里。至少对我来说，我赶上了 Figma 塞进一堆更技术性功能的这波浪潮。有一种新的设计，老实说感觉更像工程。我很轻松就能去折腾。我很好奇，就直接上手了。我试了各种小技巧，不断把想法发出去。它不是'你应该这么做'，而是'嘿，我试了这个，很酷，明天再试一次'。我觉得我们正处在一个机会再次大开的时刻，那些想在设计社群里成长的人可以抓住它。大家太渴望看到别人的工作流、看到人们在跑的 100% 不同实验、以及别人得到的经验。只要你出现、去尝试、保持好奇，然后把 Twitter 当作一本记录你所学和所做实验的小日志——现在正是收获'公开好奇'红利的时候。

turns.en: I’ve been very prescriptive with a few newer designers. They asked me, 'What should I do?' I said, 'Okay, do the thing I just said: pick a project, run an experiment, go to Twitter, share it. You don’t have to act like you’re a guru. This isn’t about being a guru. This is about—'
turns.zh: 我对最近几个更年轻的设计师给了很具体的建议。他们问我：'我该怎么做？' 我说：'好，就按我刚刚说的来：选一个项目，做一个实验，去 Twitter 上分享。你不用装成大师。这不是关于大师范儿。这是关于——'

turns.en: In fact, don’t. Yeah. Just build in public and say, 'Here’s what I did.' And here’s the thing: the posts that really pop off—if you want to talk about algo-maxing—are things like vibe-coding something very visual, something weird and unique, like a 3D graph or some 3D space-time thing, and just sharing it. It’s so easy to vibe-code for content now. But if you want it to be useful—and that’s what I’d recommend—create something specific to a workflow you want to solve for a project, then capture the visual artifact from that. There’s some moment in there that’s visually interesting; share that, plus a few bullet points on what you learned. That will farm engagement. That would work so well right now for client work and lead generation.
turns.zh: 事实上，别那样就对了。对，就公开搭建，然后说：'这是我做的。' 关键在于，真正能爆的内容——如果你想把算法吃透——就是 vibe code 一些非常视觉化的东西，一些古怪又独特的，比如 3D 图，或者某种 3D 时空的东西，然后直接分享。现在用 vibe code 产出内容太容易了。但如果你想让内容真正有用——而这也是我推荐的——就创造某个特定于你想解决的工作流的东西，然后从里面截取那个视觉产物。过程中总有一个视觉上很有趣的瞬间；把它分享出来，再加上几点你学到的要点。这就能引发互动。现在做这事对接客户、对做销售线索都非常有效。

turns.en: I don’t know if you’re seeing this—curious to hear your perspective too—but I’m starting to notice in the job market a demand. Not necessarily on paper, but a demand for designers who can help level up the rest of the org, the way they work, and their AI systems. A person who can blaze the trail, you know? And if you can position yourself that way—whether in an interview or just on your Twitter profile—it’s a massive green flag in today’s job market. Have you seen that at all?
turns.zh: 我不知道你有没有看到，也很想听听你的看法。但我在就业市场里开始注意到一种需求。不是写在岗位说明里的那种，而是对设计师的需求：他们能帮助整个组织升维，改善组织的工作方式，以及他们的 AI 系统。就是那个能开辟道路的人，你懂吧？如果你能把自己定位成这样——不管是在面试里，还是仅仅在你的 Twitter 简介上——这在今天的就业市场是一个非常非常大的加分项。你有看到过吗？

turns.en: Yeah. The thing I’ve found most interesting is internal tool building. If you’re not a designated leader at the organization, the absolute best way to get leaned on that way is to do what Brandon Engineer did at Vercel: find a cross-functional use case where design is needed by marketing, for a task you don’t have time for or don’t want to spend time on, and build an internal tool. I think they said there were 1,500 vibe-coded tools inside Ramp that they had made, right? And the question is: how much of that is throwaway? Well, most of it.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得最有趣的是内部工具搭建。如果你不是组织里指定的领导者，想成为被依赖的那种人，绝对最好的方法是学 Brandon Engineer 在 Vercel 做的事：找一个跨职能的用例，让营销团队需要设计，而对一个你没时间做、也不想花时间做的任务，去建一个内部工具。我记得他们说过，Ramp 内部有 1,500 个 vibe code 出来的工具，对吧？然后问题是：有多少是随手做的？答案是，大部分都是。

turns.en: We should have a bi-annual state of the state of perspective, you know?
turns.zh: 我们是不是该每半年做一次“视角之视角”的现状报告，你知道吗？

turns.en: I think this is the first one of those and we'll have more.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是这类活动中的第一次，以后还会有更多。

turns.en: Inspired by you, by the way, so that's where it all came from. I got you. All right, but I got you.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，这是受你启发的，这就是一切的来源。我懂你。好吧，但我懂你。

consensus.en: AI fluency will eventually become ambient, but right now it matters because companies want designers who can explore what-if questions in new ways.
consensus.zh: AI 素养终将成为常态，但当下仍很重要，因为公司需要能以全新方式探索 what-if 问题的设计师。

consensus.en: The best teams create space and budget for AI experimentation through hackathons and dedicated teams, accepting throwaway work as part of cost.
consensus.zh: 最优秀的团队通过黑客松和专项小组为 AI 实验留出空间与预算，并把一次性探索视为成本的一部分。

consensus.en: Design is moving toward a briefcase context layer: intent and context should travel with you across tools and agents.
consensus.zh: 设计正走向一种‘公文包式上下文层’：意图与上下文应随你在不同工具和智能体之间携带。

consensus.en: Designers can create high impact by building internal tools that let marketing and cross-functional partners ship without depending on design.
consensus.zh: 设计师可以通过构建内部工具产生高影响力，让市场等跨职能伙伴不再依赖设计团队就能交付。

consensus.en: The future belongs to builders; designers should embrace systems thinking and continuously compare workflows because best practices haven't converged yet.
consensus.zh: 未来属于建设者；设计师应拥抱系统思维，并持续比较工作流，因为最佳实践尚未收敛。

contrarian.en: Against the AI-slop narrative, designers who vibe code report higher workflow satisfaction; AI enables micro-precision decisions designers didn't have before.
contrarian.zh: 与‘AI 垃圾’叙事相反，进行 vibe coding 的设计师对工作流满意度更高；AI 让他们做出以往没有的微观精确决策。

contrarian.en: Fully automated agent workflows are not the goal; keeping some friction lets you fact-check intent and re-steer, making better results.
contrarian.zh: 完全自动化的智能体工作流不是目标；保留一些摩擦才能校验意图并重新调整方向，从而获得更好结果。

contrarian.en: Comparing models by one-shot prompts is meaningless; you must drive the model over many iterations to evaluate it properly.
contrarian.zh: 用一次性提示词比较模型毫无意义；你必须像驾驶一样多轮迭代，才能真正评估模型。

contrarian.en: It's okay to wait on adopting agentic tooling now; convergence will bring cheaper, easier entry later, so don't let FOMO drive you.
contrarian.zh: 现在暂缓采用智能体式工具也没关系；未来会收敛出更便宜、更易上手的入场方式，不必被 FOMO 裹挟。

contrarian.en: Managers are doing more vibe coding than junior and mid-level ICs, which may be cutting less senior designers out of the process.
contrarian.zh: 管理者的 vibe coding 参与度高于初级和中级设计师，这可能让资历较浅的设计师被排除在流程之外。

contrarian.en: You don't need to read your context or markdown files; feeding corrections and negative examples builds a reliable black-box briefcase.
contrarian.zh: 你并不需要阅读自己的上下文或 Markdown 文件；持续喂入修正和负面示例，就能构建可靠的‘黑箱公文包’。
